title: Attorney General Todd Blanche Defends White House Media Bans, Calling Press Credentials a 'Privilege, Not a Right'
snippet: Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the administration's move to restrict access for select mainstream news outlets, framing press credentials as a privilege while also detailing the Justice Department's approach to AI oversight.
content:
WASHINGTON — Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday vigorously defended the administration's decision to restrict access for several major media organizations, asserting that presence inside the White House press room is 'a privilege... not a right.'

Appearing on ABC's This Week, Blanche pushed back against assertions that President Donald Trump had improperly revoked credentials from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. Instead, Blanche characterized the move as a response to persistent coverage that the administration deems inaccurate.

'The president hasn't denied access. That's not the right way to describe it,' Blanche told anchor Martha Raddatz. He asserted that inaccuracies in reporting from major outlets pose a broader 'national security problem' by distorting information meant for both the public and foreign partners.

Legal Pushback and Travel Access Controversies

Blanche's comments come amid an ongoing legal standoff over the restrictions. Late last week, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the outlets' hard passes. In his ruling, Kelly expressed skepticism regarding the administration's national security justification, noting that President Trump's public explanations focused largely on personal frustration with negative coverage over the past two years.

Though journalists were initially allowed back on White House grounds following the judge's order, tensions flared again over the weekend when CNN was barred from joining the press pool aboard Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee. Blanche dismissed concerns over the exclusion, arguing that administration officials routinely decide which reporters travel with the president.

'It's not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it's common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel,' Blanche stated.

DOJ Stance on Artificial Intelligence

During the interview, Blanche also outlined the Department of Justice's strategy regarding artificial intelligence, reinforcing President Trump's position that maintaining American dominance in AI technology against global competitors like China is paramount.

Despite recent global security concerns and reports of AI models interacting unexpectedly with government websites, Blanche rejected calls for sweeping new federal regulations that could slow technological development.

'The answer isn't always more laws, more laws, more laws,' Blanche said, maintaining that existing federal criminal codes under Title 18 provide sufficient authority for the DOJ, FBI, and Homeland Security Investigations to prosecute bad actors in the AI space without stymieing industry growth.
